title: The Paradox of the Third Particle is classical
abstract: The Paradox of the Third Particle arises when particles are described relative to one of them serving as a reference frame. Although it is typically attributed to quantum superpositions, we show that the paradox and its ramifications$\unicode{x2014}$such as the relativity of subsystems$\unicode{x2014}$already occur classically. In light of this insight, we establish a no-go theorem that holds whenever physical subsystems, whether classical or quantum, are used as reference frames: if one demands that frame transformations be information-preserving, then it is impossible to meaningfully partition the world into subsystems, like individual particles, from the perspective of each frame.
summary: This theoretical paper analyzes the 'Paradox of the Third Particle' by extending its analysis from quantum mechanics into classical mechanics. The authors prove a no-go theorem demonstrating that any consistent physical theory describing subsystems relative to different reference frames must violate at least one fundamental principle (like information preservation or relationality). This suggests deep constraints on how we can mathematically partition and describe reality across multiple perspectives.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether the 'Paradox of the Third Particle,' typically discussed in quantum mechanics regarding reference frames, persists when considering classical systems.
main_result: A no-go theorem is established showing that if one demands information-preserving frame transformations for physical subsystems (classical or quantum), it is impossible to meaningfully partition the world into independent subsystems from every perspective.
method: The authors analyze both quantum and classical analogues of reference frame transformations, using joint probability distributions (classical) or density operators/unitary transformations (quantum). They establish consistency conditions based on three postulates: Geometry, Position/momentum separation, and Information preservation.
model_or_system: The system involves three particles (A, B, C) whose states are described by phase space coordinates (classically) or quantum states. The analysis focuses on how the description of one particle depends on a reference frame defined by another.
key_observables: Information retrieval success probability ($P_{succ}$), joint probability distributions $P(A)_{BM}$, and the consistency of state descriptions across different perspectives (the 'atlas of perspectives').
important_parameters: The number of particles (three is central), the nature of the reference frame transformation ($ ar{T}_{A	o B}$), and the assumption of information preservation.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that reference frames are physical systems, leading to postulates defining the transformations, most critically the requirement that these transformations must be information-preserving (symplectomorphisms classically, unitaries quantum mechanically).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the paradox using state dependence on a third particle and show geometric intuition for frame transformations in both quantum and classical settings.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the paradox in the quantum setting, then extends the analysis to a fully classical framework. It develops a no-go theorem by showing that maintaining information preservation forces a violation of either relationality or decomposability when comparing different perspectives.
why_interesting: This work tackles fundamental issues regarding the structure of physical reality and measurement theory, which underpins how we model quantum systems relative to observers/reference frames. It challenges foundational assumptions about locality and separability in physics.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Quantum Paradox of the Third Particle. From the perspective of one particle (dotted), the state of other particles (solid) depends on the value m of a bit. From A’s perspective, the state of particle B is the same independently of whether the third particle C is ignored, as in (a), or included in the description, as in (b). The paradox arises because, after transforming to B’s perspective (vertical arrow), the state of A is different depending on whether C is considered. This difference is operationally relevant: in (a), the value m is retrievable by acting on A only, whereas this is not the case in (b).

Figure 3: Geometric intuition. The upper part shows the perspective from particle A (dotted) on particles B and C (solid). The lower part shows the perspective from particle B (dotted) on particles A and C (solid). The reference frame transformation ¯T A→B from A’s perspective to B’s perspective corresponds to a shift of the origin from the location of A to the location of B.

Figure 4: The classical Paradox of the Third Particle. From A’s perspective, B’s state depends on the value m of the bit M, regardless of whether the third particle C is ignored, as in (a), or included, as in (b). However, upon transforming to B’s perspective, a discrepancy arises: the state of A depends on m if C is ignored when transforming, as on the right-hand side of (a), whereas it is independent of m if C is accounted for, as in (c).

Figure 6: Heisenberg cuts. Originally, the notion of a Heisenberg cut was introduced in quantum theory as the boundary between the world described by quantum theory and the rest. Here, we use this notion more generally: the boundary between the systems described from a perspective and the rest. Figure (a) shows the case relevant to the Paradox of the Third Particle, and Figure (b) the standard situation.
